lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon: Why Does Kipchoge Recover So Fast?

quiz.prompt: A data sheet shows the heart-rate recovery of an elite marathon runner (illustrative curve). His heart rate was 172 beats per minute (bpm) at the finish and about 100 bpm roughly 4 minutes later. By about how many bpm did it fall in those 4 minutes?
choices: 100 bpm
82 bpm
72 bpm
62 bpm
quiz.rationale: Reading the data: 172 - 100 = 72 bpm. This checks that learners can read values from the recovery data before predicting.
quiz.placement: Predict: half-page data sheet with Curve A (elite marathon runner) and Curve B (average healthy teenager)

quiz.prompt: Learners wrote 'I notice...' and 'I predict...' statements about two heart-rate recovery curves. Which of these is an OBSERVATION from the data rather than a prediction?
choices: The elite runner's blood carries more oxygen than the teenager's blood.
The elite runner's heart rate was about 100 bpm four minutes after finishing.
The elite runner has a bigger heart than the teenager.
The teenager recovers slowly because he does not practise running.
quiz.rationale: An observation states what the data show. The heart rate being about 100 bpm after four minutes is read directly from the curve. The other choices are guesses about causes, which are predictions that still need testing.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Write-Pair-Share 'I notice...' and 'I predict that the difference is caused by...'

quiz.prompt: In the teacher's account, a tilapia in Lake Victoria, a frog in the Rift Valley wetlands and a goat at Gikomba market have hearts with different numbers of chambers. Which list gives the numbers of chambers correctly?
choices: Tilapia 4, frog 3, goat 2
Tilapia 2, frog 4, goat 4
Tilapia 3, frog 2, goat 4
Tilapia 2, frog 3, goat 4
quiz.rationale: The account gives the tilapia a two-chambered heart, the frog three chambers and the goat four chambers, like humans. The grasshopper has no heart like Kipchoge's.
quiz.placement: Observe: grasshopper, tilapia, frog and goat comparison

quiz.prompt: After hearing about the grasshopper, tilapia, frog and goat, a learner asks: 'Does having more heart chambers mean being a better animal?' At this point in the inquiry, which response is most appropriate?
choices: This has not been explained yet; it is a good question to investigate using evidence in later lessons.
Only animals with four chambers need a transport system.
No, the number of chambers makes no difference to any animal.
Yes, more chambers always make an animal better.
quiz.rationale: This is the anchoring lesson, so the phenomenon is left unexplained. The class records the question and investigates it over the coming lessons rather than accepting or rejecting an answer now.
quiz.placement: Observe: pair talk 'Does having more heart chambers mean being a better animal?'

quiz.prompt: Two learners give different explanations for the same heart-rate data. What is the scientific way to decide between them?
choices: Choose the explanation given by the learner who speaks first.
Find out which explanation the evidence supports best.
Accept the teacher's guess without testing it.
Choose the explanation that most learners prefer.
quiz.rationale: The lesson models linking claims to evidence: different explanations are normal, and the class investigates which one the evidence best supports. Popularity or order of speaking does not decide it.
quiz.placement: Explain: 'My current explanation (Iteration 1)' and 'Claims to investigate' on the board

quiz.prompt: The class Driving Question Board has two columns: 'What we notice' and 'What we wonder'. Which card belongs under 'What we wonder'?
choices: Omondi's heart rate was still 90 bpm fifteen minutes after jogging 400 m.
Kipchoge's heart rate fell to about 100 bpm within about four minutes.
Why does a grasshopper not have a pump like ours?
A tilapia has a two-chambered heart.
quiz.rationale: A 'wonder' is a question about something not yet understood. The other three cards are facts from the data or the story, so they belong under 'What we notice'.
quiz.placement: DQB: yellow 'notice' cards and blue 'wonder' cards on the Driving Question Board

quiz.prompt: In the first lesson on Animal Transport, learners state a basic idea about why animals have transport systems. Which statement best describes the job of a transport system in an animal?
choices: It is found only in animals that have a heart with four chambers.
It moves substances such as oxygen, nutrients and wastes around the body.
It makes the animal run faster than other animals.
It only keeps the animal's body warm.
quiz.rationale: The lesson's knowledge outcome is that animals need transport systems to move substances around their bodies. How different animals do this is left for later lessons.
quiz.placement: Model: 'My Transport System Model - Iteration 1' sketch of how substances move inside an animal

lessons.title: Why Can't Large Animals Just Use Diffusion? — The Importance of Transport Systems

quiz.prompt: An amoeba is about 0.1 mm across. A cluster of human leg muscle cells lies several centimetres deep below the skin. For which one is diffusion alone enough to supply oxygen, and why?
choices: The amoeba, because oxygen only has to diffuse a very short distance to reach all parts of the cell
Both, because diffusion works at the same speed over any distance
Neither, because every living thing needs a heart to move oxygen
The muscle cells, because they are made of many cells and so have more surface area in total
quiz.rationale: Diffusion is fast over very short distances, so a tiny amoeba can be supplied directly from its surroundings. Cells several centimetres below the skin are too far away for diffusion to supply them in time.
quiz.placement: Predict: amoeba-vs-muscle diagram prediction ('For which organism is diffusion sufficient, and why?')

quiz.prompt: In Activity A, a group makes a cube with sides of 3 cm. Using Surface Area = 6 × side² and Volume = side³, what is the SA:V ratio of this cube?
quiz.rationale: Surface area = 6 × 3² = 54 cm². Volume = 3³ = 27 cm³. SA:V = 54 ÷ 27 = 2.
quiz.placement: Activity A: SA:V ratio modelling with 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm cubes

quiz.prompt: A 1 cm cube has an SA:V ratio of 6. A 3 cm cube has an SA:V ratio of 2. What does this suggest about a large animal compared with a small one?
choices: The two animals have the same SA:V ratio, so both can rely on diffusion
The large animal has less surface area for each unit of volume, so diffusion alone cannot supply all its cells
The large animal has more surface area for each unit of volume, so diffusion is faster in it
The large animal has a smaller volume, so its cells are closer to the surface
quiz.rationale: As size increases, volume grows faster than surface area, so SA:V falls. A large body has less surface for each unit of volume, and many of its cells are far from the surface, so it needs a transport system.
quiz.placement: Activity A: SA:V ratio modelling ('As the cube gets bigger, what happens to the SA:V ratio?')

quiz.prompt: In Activity B, a learner counts 45 pulse beats in 30 seconds immediately after star jumps. What is the pulse rate in beats per minute (BPM)?
choices: 75 BPM
45 BPM
90 BPM
22.5 BPM
quiz.rationale: The count was for 30 seconds, so multiply by 2 to get beats per minute: 45 × 2 = 90 BPM.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Pulse rate and breathing rate measurement (count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2)

quiz.prompt: Kipchoge's quadriceps muscles are about 8 cm below the skin. Why could oxygen NOT reach these muscle cells by diffusion alone from the skin during a marathon?
choices: The skin is waterproof, so no oxygen can ever enter the body
Diffusion only moves carbon dioxide, not oxygen
The muscles are pumping too hard for oxygen to enter them
Diffusion time increases greatly with distance, so it would take hours instead of the seconds the muscles need
quiz.rationale: Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance. It is fast over fractions of a millimetre but takes many hours across several centimetres, far too slow for working muscle.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER discussion, 'how long would oxygen take to diffuse from his skin to that muscle cell?'

quiz.prompt: At km 30 of a marathon, Kipchoge's leg muscles release a lot of heat. His blood carries this heat to other parts of the body so he does not overheat. Which transport function is this?
choices: Delivery of nutrients
Immune defence
Transport of hormones
Thermoregulation (redistributing heat)
quiz.rationale: Moving heat made by working muscles around the body so that it can be lost is thermoregulation, one of the five transport functions.
quiz.placement: Explain: annotating the body-outline diagram linking each transport function to a Kipchoge marathon scenario

quiz.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'Without a transport system, Kipchoge's muscle cells would ________ because ________.'
choices: stop needing oxygen, because a large body has a high SA:V ratio
run out of oxygen and glucose and build up CO₂, because diffusion is too slow over the large distance from the skin
work normally, because the heart only pumps harder and is not needed to move substances
get too much oxygen, because diffusion is fast over long distances
quiz.rationale: Deep muscle cells need a constant supply of oxygen and glucose and removal of CO₂. Diffusion over a large distance is too slow to do this, so a transport system is needed.
quiz.placement: Model: cumulative model revision, sentence stem 'Without a transport system, Kipchoge's muscle cells would ________ because ________'

lessons.title: Transport in Insects: The Open Circulatory System of the Grasshopper

quiz.prompt: A group dissects a grasshopper to find the dorsal vessel, which acts as its simple pump. Where do they find it?
choices: Running along the belly, close to the legs
Coiled inside each leg
Running along the back of the body, under the upper surface
Inside the head only, behind the eyes
quiz.rationale: The dorsal vessel is a tube-like pump that runs along the back (dorsal side) of the grasshopper. Learners find it by cutting along the dorsal midline.
quiz.placement: Activity A — Dissection or Diagram: Task 1, identify the dorsal vessel running along the back

quiz.prompt: A student cuts open a grasshopper and sees that its haemolymph is pale yellow-green, not red. What does this colour show?
choices: The grasshopper has been dead so long that its blood has lost its colour
The haemolymph carries oxygen using a red pigment that has faded
The haemolymph carries more oxygen than human blood does
The haemolymph has no haemoglobin, so it does not carry oxygen to the cells
quiz.rationale: Red colour in human blood comes from haemoglobin, which carries oxygen. Pale haemolymph has no haemoglobin, so it does not transport oxygen in insects.
quiz.placement: Activity A — Dissection or Diagram: Task 4, note the colour of haemolymph (pale yellow-green, not red)

quiz.prompt: A group looks for blood vessels branching from the dorsal vessel of a grasshopper to its legs and organs, and finds none. What is the best explanation?
choices: The haemolymph flows out into an open body cavity (haemocoel) and bathes the organs directly
The vessels are too small to see, but the grasshopper has a closed system like Kipchoge's
The haemolymph stays inside the dorsal vessel and never reaches the organs
The vessels were destroyed when the grasshopper was killed
quiz.rationale: The grasshopper has an open circulatory system. There are no vessels branching to organs, and haemolymph fills the haemocoel and bathes the organs directly.
quiz.placement: Activity A — Dissection or Diagram: Task 3, observe that there are NO distinct blood vessels branching to organs

quiz.prompt: The dorsal vessel of a grasshopper has tiny paired slits along it called ostia. What is their function?
choices: They let oxygen from the air enter the dorsal vessel
They let waste leave the body
They are entry points that let haemolymph from the haemocoel flow into the dorsal vessel
They let the dorsal vessel attach to the muscles of the legs
quiz.rationale: Ostia are the entry points for haemolymph. Haemolymph in the haemocoel enters the dorsal vessel through them, and closed systems have no equivalent.
quiz.placement: Activity A — Dissection or Diagram: Task 2, look for the ostia with a hand lens or use the labelled diagram

quiz.prompt: In insects such as the grasshopper, haemolymph does not carry oxygen. How do the body cells get their oxygen?
choices: Oxygen dissolves in haemolymph and is pumped to cells by the dorsal vessel
Oxygen is absorbed through the mouth and carried in the food
Oxygen enters through the ostia and is carried by haemoglobin
The tracheal system delivers oxygen directly to the cells
quiz.rationale: Insects use a tracheal system for gas exchange, which handles oxygen directly. Haemolymph transports other substances, not oxygen.
quiz.placement: Whole-class CER discussion: key conceptual target (2) — insects do NOT use haemolymph for oxygen transport

quiz.prompt: Which statement best explains why a grasshopper's circulatory system could NOT support a body running a marathon like Eliud Kipchoge?
choices: Its open, low-pressure system cannot direct large amounts of oxygen-rich blood to working muscles
Its haemolymph is too red and thick to flow quickly
Its dorsal vessel has too many chambers, which slows the flow
It has no dorsal vessel, so nothing pumps the haemolymph
quiz.rationale: In an open system haemolymph bathes organs directly at low pressure, with no capillaries, and it does not carry oxygen. It cannot deliver oxygen-rich blood to specific muscles during intense exercise, as Kipchoge's closed system does.
quiz.placement: Whole-class CER discussion: 'Could the grasshopper's circulatory system support Eliud Kipchoge running a marathon?'

quiz.prompt: A learner adds the grasshopper's dorsal vessel to their cumulative model and compares it to the human heart. Which annotation is correct?
choices: A large muscular organ in the head that pumps blood to the legs
A simple tube-like pump divided into segments, not four chambers
A heart with no chambers that pumps red blood through closed vessels
A four-chambered heart, the same as a human heart
quiz.rationale: The dorsal vessel is a simple tube-like pump divided into segments. It is not a four-chambered heart and does not pump red blood through closed vessels.
quiz.placement: Cumulative model update: grasshopper panel, annotation (1) for the dorsal vessel and the comparison arrow to the human system

lessons.title: Transport in Fish — The Single Circulatory System of the Tilapia

quiz.prompt: In an earlier lesson you studied the transport system of the grasshopper. Which statement correctly describes it?
choices: It is an open system in which haemolymph flows freely around the organs in the body cavity.
It is a closed system with a two-chambered heart made of one atrium and one ventricle.
It is a single circuit in which blood goes from the heart to the gills, then to the body, then back to the heart.
It is a closed system in which blood stays inside vessels and is pumped through a four-chambered heart.
quiz.rationale: The grasshopper has an open haemolymph system, so the fluid is not kept inside vessels all the time. The other choices describe closed systems of fish or mammals.
quiz.placement: Predict: tilapia image and prediction task (retrieval of the grasshopper's open system from Lesson 3)

quiz.prompt: How many chambers does the heart of a tilapia have?
choices: Three chambers: two atria and one ventricle
One chamber: a simple tube with no atrium or ventricle
Two chambers: one atrium and one ventricle
Four chambers: two atria and two ventricles
quiz.rationale: The tilapia heart is two-chambered, with one atrium and one ventricle. Four chambers belong to the mammalian heart, and a simple tube-like heart is not what the fish diagram shows.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Diagram Tracing (labelling the two-chambered fish heart)

quiz.prompt: Which sequence shows the path of blood in the single circulatory system of a tilapia, starting at the heart?
choices: Heart → gill capillaries → heart → body tissues → heart
Heart → body tissues → gill capillaries → heart
Heart → body tissues → heart, with the blood oxygenated inside the heart
Heart → gill capillaries (oxygenated here) → body tissues → veins → back to the heart
quiz.rationale: Blood leaves the heart, is oxygenated at the gill capillaries, travels via the dorsal aorta to the body tissues, then returns by veins to the heart in one loop. Oxygenation happens at the gills, not in the heart, and blood does not return to the heart between the gills and the body.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Diagram Tracing (red and blue tracing of the single circuit)

quiz.prompt: In a tilapia, blood passes through the gill capillaries before going to the body tissues. What happens to the blood pressure after the gill capillaries, and what does this mean for the tissues?
choices: Blood pressure drops, but a second ventricle pumps the blood again before it reaches the tissues.
Blood pressure drops significantly, so the tissues receive blood at a lower pressure than in a mammal.
Blood pressure rises because the gills pump the blood, so the tissues receive blood at a higher pressure than in a mammal.
Blood pressure stays the same as when it left the heart, because no pressure is lost in the gills.
quiz.rationale: The tilapia has only one ventricle, so blood is not pumped again after the gills. The pressure falls and the tissues receive blood at lower pressure than in a mammal.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Reading + Data (the sentence about blood pressure after the gill capillaries)

quiz.prompt: Both a Nile tilapia and Eliud Kipchoge need oxygen delivered to their muscles. Which is one structural reason Kipchoge's circulatory system delivers oxygen more efficiently?
choices: In the tilapia heart, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, but in mammals they do not.
In mammals, blood returns from the lungs to the heart and is pumped a second time at high pressure to the body, whereas in the tilapia blood goes to the body at lower pressure after the gills.
His heart has only one chamber, so blood can move through it faster than in a fish.
His blood flows in open spaces around the organs, so it reaches every cell directly.
quiz.rationale: The mammalian double circulation re-pressurises the blood after the lungs. In the tilapia's single circuit the pressure drops after the gills and is not restored. Only deoxygenated blood enters the fish heart, so mixing is not the reason.
quiz.placement: Part B: Explanation Writing (one structural reason Kipchoge's system is more efficient)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the transport system of a grasshopper with that of a tilapia?
choices: Both have closed systems with the same number of heart chambers.
Both have open systems, but the tilapia has a heart with two chambers.
The grasshopper has a closed system and the tilapia has an open system.
The tilapia's blood stays inside vessels all the time, while the grasshopper's haemolymph flows in the open body cavity.
quiz.rationale: The tilapia has a closed system with a two-chambered heart and blood always in vessels. The grasshopper has an open system with haemolymph bathing the organs.
quiz.placement: Part A: Comparative Table Construction (Insect vs Fish columns: open/closed, blood vessel types)

quiz.prompt: A learner writes an 'efficiency rating' for the tilapia's circulatory system on their model. Which claim is best supported by the evidence from this lesson?
choices: As efficient as a mammal's system because both are closed systems with blood in vessels.
More efficient than a mammal's system because the blood makes only one circuit around the body.
More efficient than the grasshopper because blood stays in vessels, but less efficient than a mammal because blood pressure drops after the gills.
Less efficient than the grasshopper because the tilapia heart has only one atrium.
quiz.rationale: The tilapia's closed system is more efficient than the grasshopper's open system. However, its single circuit has no second pumping after the gills, so pressure falls and it is less efficient than the mammal's double circulation.
quiz.placement: Cumulative Model Revision: (c) one-sentence 'efficiency rating' next to the fish system

lessons.title: Transport in Amphibians and Reptiles — The Trade-Off Heart

quiz.prompt: How many chambers does the heart of a frog have, and how are they arranged?
choices: Two atria and one ventricle
One atrium and one ventricle
One atrium and two ventricles
Two atria and two ventricles
quiz.rationale: The amphibian heart is three-chambered: a right atrium, a left atrium and a single ventricle. Two atria and two ventricles describes the four-chambered mammalian heart.
quiz.placement: Part A: Heart Comparison Resource Card (Frog three-chambered heart)

quiz.prompt: In a frog's heart, oxygenated blood from the left atrium and deoxygenated blood from the right atrium both empty into one ventricle. What happens to the blood there?
choices: All the blood becomes fully oxygenated before leaving the heart
All the blood becomes deoxygenated before leaving the heart
The two kinds of blood mix, so blood sent to the body is only partly oxygenated
The two kinds of blood stay completely separate, so the body receives fully oxygenated blood
quiz.rationale: There is only one ventricle, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix (the purple arrows). The body therefore receives partly oxygenated blood.
quiz.placement: Part B: Blood Flow Tracing Activity (frog diagram)

quiz.prompt: In the blood-flow diagrams, red arrows show oxygenated blood and blue arrows show deoxygenated blood. A purple arrow inside a ventricle shows that the blood there is...
choices: fully oxygenated blood
blood that has stopped moving
fully deoxygenated blood
a mixture of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
quiz.rationale: Purple is made by combining red and blue, so it shows mixed blood. This is how the lesson makes blood mixing visible.
quiz.placement: Part A: Observation Table, 'Does blood mix?' column

quiz.prompt: Which row correctly shows whether blood mixes in each heart?
choices: Frog: No. Nile monitor lizard: Partial.
Frog: Yes. Nile monitor lizard: No.
Frog: Yes. Nile monitor lizard: Partial.
Frog: Partial. Nile monitor lizard: Yes.
quiz.rationale: The frog has a single undivided ventricle, so blood mixes. The lizard has a partly divided ventricle, which reduces mixing but does not remove it.
quiz.placement: Part A: Observation Table, 'Does blood mix?' column

quiz.prompt: A table gives illustrative oxygen-delivery scores out of 100: tilapia 80, frog 65, monitor lizard 75, human 98. Which animal has the lowest score, and what is the best explanation?
choices: The monitor lizard, because its ventricle is partly divided
The human, because a four-chambered heart mixes blood the most
The tilapia, because fish have no heart
The frog, because its single ventricle mixes oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood
quiz.rationale: The frog scores 65, the lowest. Its single ventricle mixes the two blood streams. The scores are estimates, not measured values.
quiz.placement: Part C: Data Table Analysis (bar graph, circle the lowest score)

quiz.prompt: What does the partial septum in the ventricle of a reptile such as the Nile monitor lizard do?
choices: It stops mixing of blood completely
It reduces mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood but does not stop it completely
It increases mixing of blood compared with a frog
It stores oxygen for the heart
quiz.rationale: The partial division keeps the two blood streams partly apart, so reptiles mix less than frogs, but mixing still happens. The circulation is incomplete.
quiz.placement: Part A: Structured Notes with Gaps (reptile partial septum)

quiz.prompt: Why can a Rift Valley frog survive with a three-chambered heart that mixes blood?
choices: Its blood is completely oxygenated even though it mixes
It is endothermic, so it needs very little oxygen
It never needs oxygen because it has moist skin
It is ectothermic, so it uses little energy to make body heat and has a low oxygen demand
quiz.rationale: Ectotherms do not use energy to keep their bodies warm, so their oxygen demand is low. Partly oxygenated blood is enough for them.
quiz.placement: Part B: Trade-Off Discussion ('A frog does not need a four-chambered heart because...')

quiz.prompt: Which statement best explains why a Rift Valley frog could not run a 42 km marathon, even if its legs were strong enough?
choices: Its blood contains no oxygen at all
Its heart has four chambers, which slows the blood down
Its heart pumps oxygenated blood and deoxygenated blood completely separately, which wastes energy
Mixed blood in its single ventricle gives muscles too little oxygen for the high oxygen demand of long, fast running
quiz.rationale: Because the ventricle mixes the blood, the muscles receive partly oxygenated blood. That cannot supply the high oxygen demand of marathon running.
quiz.placement: Part C: Application Question (Rift Valley frog and the 42 km marathon)

quiz.prompt: Complete the model sentence: 'As the heart becomes more chambered and blood mixing decreases, the efficiency of oxygen delivery to tissues ___.'
choices: decreases, because the blood no longer carries oxygen
decreases, because more oxygen-rich blood reaches the tissues
increases, because more oxygen-rich blood reaches the tissues
stays the same, because every heart delivers the same oxygen
quiz.rationale: Less mixing means the blood sent to the body is more highly oxygenated, so oxygen delivery becomes more efficient.
quiz.placement: Model Explanation Sentence (revising the Animal Transport System Model)

quiz.prompt: Which statement best sums up the lesson's idea that 'simpler' does not mean 'inferior' for a frog's heart?
choices: Frogs are not able to survive in the wild with such a heart
A three-chambered heart works better than a four-chambered heart in every animal
Frogs have not evolved yet, so their hearts are unfinished
Each heart design is a trade-off that suits the animal's environment and energy needs
quiz.rationale: The three-chambered heart meets a frog's low energy demand, while a high-energy animal like Kipchoge needs a more efficient four-chambered heart. Each is a trade-off suited to the animal.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board update: 'Could Kipchoge survive with a frog's heart?'

lessons.title: Transport in Mammals — The Four-Chambered Heart (Heart Dissection and Circuit Mapping)

quiz.prompt: A group squeezes the walls of a sheep heart gently. The wall of the left ventricle feels much thicker and firmer than the wall of the right ventricle. What is the best explanation?
choices: The right ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, so it needs a thinner wall to move faster.
The left ventricle is closer to the lungs, so it needs a thicker wall to push blood a short distance.
The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body, so it needs to generate higher pressure.
The left ventricle holds deoxygenated blood, which makes its wall thicker.
quiz.rationale: The left ventricle sends blood through the systemic circuit to the whole body, which needs greater pressure. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs, so its wall is thinner.
quiz.placement: Step 1: external surface and squeeze test for wall thickness

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'Arteries always carry oxygenated blood and veins always carry deoxygenated blood.' Which statement about the vessels of the mammalian heart shows that this is wrong?
choices: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The pulmonary vein carries deoxygenated blood from the lungs to the right atrium.
The aorta carries deoxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
quiz.rationale: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood back. Whether a vessel is an artery or a vein depends on the direction of flow, not on the oxygen content.
quiz.placement: Step 4: locating and comparing the pulmonary artery and aorta

quiz.prompt: A learner probes the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle of a sheep heart with a pencil. What is this valve called, and what does it do?
choices: The semilunar valve; it separates oxygenated blood from deoxygenated blood.
The bicuspid valve; it lets blood flow from the aorta into the left ventricle.
The tricuspid valve; it lets blood flow from the left ventricle back into the left atrium.
The bicuspid valve; it stops blood flowing backwards from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
quiz.rationale: The bicuspid (mitral) valve is on the left side between the atrium and the ventricle. It closes when the ventricle contracts so that blood cannot flow backwards.
quiz.placement: Step 3: probing the atrioventricular valves and chordae tendineae

quiz.prompt: Learners trace the systemic circuit with a red pen. Which pathway is correct, starting from the left ventricle?
choices: Left ventricle → aorta → body tissues → vena cava → right atrium
Right ventricle → aorta → body tissues → vena cava → left atrium
Left ventricle → vena cava → body tissues → aorta → right atrium
Left ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium
quiz.rationale: In the systemic circuit, oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the aorta, delivers oxygen to the body tissues, and returns through the vena cava to the right atrium.
quiz.placement: Step 5: colour-coded arrows tracing the pulmonary and systemic circuits

quiz.prompt: In the mammalian heart, the septum completely separates the left and right sides. Why does this make the heart more efficient than a frog heart?
choices: The septum makes the heart beat faster, so more blood is made.
The septum means a mammal has more blood in its body than a frog.
The septum lets deoxygenated blood go straight to the body to save time.
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix, so the tissues receive fully oxygenated blood.
quiz.rationale: Because the septum stops mixing, the blood sent to the muscles is fully oxygenated, so more oxygen arrives per heartbeat. Efficiency depends on what happens to the blood, not on the amount of blood.
quiz.placement: Circuit summary, sentence 3: why the septum makes the mammalian heart more efficient

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 5 we learned that mixed blood in the frog heart is acceptable. Why is mixed blood NOT good enough for a marathon runner such as Eliud Kipchoge?
choices: A frog's blood has no oxygen in it, but a mammal's blood does.
Kipchoge has a special heart that other mammals do not have.
A runner's muscles need a very high oxygen supply for hours, so the blood must reach them fully oxygenated.
A frog's heart is much bigger than a human heart, so it can mix blood safely.
quiz.rationale: Frogs have low energy demands, so partly mixed blood is enough. A runner at 21 km/h for over two hours needs the maximum oxygen per heartbeat, and the four-chambered heart that every mammal has provides this.
quiz.placement: Comparison question: 'What is different about Kipchoge?' (think-pair-share)

quiz.prompt: While drawing the mammalian heart in a cumulative model, a learner shows the pulmonary vein entering the right atrium. Which correction is right?
choices: The pulmonary vein should enter the left atrium, because it brings oxygenated blood from the lungs.
The pulmonary vein should enter the aorta directly, because it carries blood to the body.
The pulmonary vein should enter the right ventricle, ready to pump blood to the lungs.
The pulmonary vein should enter the right atrium from the body, so no correction is needed.
quiz.rationale: The pulmonary vein brings blood that has just picked up oxygen in the lungs. This blood enters the left atrium, then passes to the left ventricle to be pumped to the whole body.
quiz.placement: Cumulative model revision: adding the four-chambered heart with named vessels

lessons.title: Pumping Mechanism of the Mammalian Heart: The Cardiac Cycle, Heart Sounds, and the SAN

quiz.prompt: Before the cardiac cycle is taught, a learner is asked what happens inside the heart with each beat. Which prediction is correct?
choices: The heart sucks blood in like a sponge and the blood leaves by itself, without any squeezing
The muscular walls of the heart squeeze to push blood out, and valves keep the blood moving in one direction
The valves are the parts that pump the blood, while the heart muscle stays still
The heart squeezes in all directions, so valves are not needed
quiz.rationale: The heart is a muscular pump. Its walls contract to push blood out, and valves open and close to stop backflow. The idea that the heart only sucks blood in is the misconception to investigate.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share prediction sketch: what happens inside the heart during ONE beat

quiz.prompt: A learner presses two fingers on the inside of her wrist and counts 38 pulse beats in 30 seconds. What is her heart rate in beats per minute (BPM)?
choices: 76 BPM
19 BPM
38 BPM
114 BPM
quiz.rationale: 30 seconds is half a minute, so double the count: 38 × 2 = 76 BPM.
quiz.placement: Activity 1: Pulse Rate Investigation (resting vs. post-exercise recovery)

quiz.prompt: After 2 minutes of star jumps, a learner wants to measure her pulse correctly. Which method is best?
choices: Count the beats for any length of time and write down the number without doubling or timing
Press lightly with two fingers on the radial pulse (wrist) or carotid pulse (neck) and count for a timed 30 seconds immediately after stopping
Wait 10 minutes to rest so the pulse is easy to find, then count for 30 seconds
Press hard with the thumb on the wrist, because the thumb gives the strongest pulse
quiz.rationale: Two fingers should be used because the thumb has its own pulse. The count must be timed, here 30 seconds then doubled, and taken immediately after exercise so the post-exercise rate is recorded.
quiz.placement: Activity 1: Pulse Rate Investigation (finger placement and post-exercise counts)

quiz.prompt: The heart makes a 'lub-dub' sound. The 'lub' is the closing of the bicuspid and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole. What causes the 'dub'?
choices: The opening of the bicuspid and tricuspid valves as the ventricles fill
The heart muscle knocking against the ribs
The closing of the aortic and pulmonary semi-lunar valves at the end of ventricular systole
The atria contracting against the ventricles
quiz.rationale: The second sound is made when the semi-lunar valves in the aorta and pulmonary artery snap shut at the end of ventricular systole, stopping blood from flowing back into the ventricles.
quiz.placement: Activity 2: Heart Sounds Simulation ('Lub-Dub')

quiz.prompt: At rest, one complete cardiac cycle takes 0.8 seconds (atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, diastole 0.4 s). How many cardiac cycles (heartbeats) happen in one minute?
choices: 75 beats per minute
80 beats per minute
48 beats per minute
0.8 beats per minute
quiz.rationale: There are 60 seconds in a minute, so 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats per minute.
quiz.placement: Cardiac cycle timeline on the board: calculating beats per minute from a 0.8 s cycle

quiz.prompt: During a race, an athlete's heart beats 170 times per minute. About how long does one complete cardiac cycle last?
choices: About 2.8 seconds
About 0.35 seconds
About 0.8 seconds
About 110 seconds
quiz.rationale: One minute is 60 seconds, so each cycle lasts 60 ÷ 170 ≈ 0.35 seconds. This is much shorter than the 0.8 s at rest.
quiz.placement: Cardiac cycle timeline on the board: cycle length at Kipchoge's racing rate of 170 BPM

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the sino-atrial node (SAN)?
choices: It is a nerve in the brain that must send a signal before every single heartbeat
It is a valve between the right atrium and right ventricle that makes the 'lub' sound
It is a blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart
It is a patch of specialised muscle in the right atrium wall that generates its own electrical impulse and sets the rhythm of the heart
quiz.rationale: The SAN is the heart's pacemaker. It fires by itself, and the impulse spreads across the atria and then to the ventricles. Nerve signals and adrenaline only adjust its rate.
quiz.placement: Introduction of the SINO-ATRIAL NODE (SAN) and the conductor analogy

quiz.prompt: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. A trained athlete has a resting heart rate of 50 beats per minute and a cardiac output of 5 litres (5000 mL) per minute. What is her stroke volume?
choices: 5050 mL per beat
10 mL per beat
250 mL per beat
100 mL per beat
quiz.rationale: Stroke volume = cardiac output ÷ heart rate = 5000 mL ÷ 50 = 100 mL per beat. A larger stroke volume means fewer beats are needed to deliver the same output.
quiz.placement: Cardiac output calculation: stroke volume for Kipchoge and an average student

quiz.prompt: After exercise stops, a trained runner's heart rate falls quickly. Which explanation is best?
choices: A large stroke volume alone makes the heart rate drop quickly after exercise
Nerve signals that slow the SAN take over again from adrenaline, and trained muscles use oxygen efficiently so less extra blood is needed
The valves close permanently until the runner has rested
The SAN stops firing for a few minutes so the heart can rest
quiz.rationale: Adrenaline speeds up the SAN during exercise. Once exercise stops, nerve signals slow the SAN again, and efficient trained muscles need less extra blood. Stroke volume explains the low resting rate but not how quickly the rate falls.
quiz.placement: Model Narration, Sentence 3: why Kipchoge's heart recovers faster than ours

lessons.title: The Lymphatic System: The Hidden Highway of Animal Transport

quiz.prompt: Blood is pumped through capillaries under pressure. A small amount of plasma leaks out of the blood capillaries into the spaces between body cells. What is this leaked fluid called when it is still in the spaces between the cells?
choices: Lymph
Tissue fluid
Haemolymph
Serum from the kidneys
quiz.rationale: Plasma that leaks from blood capillaries into the spaces between cells is called tissue fluid. It is only called lymph after it has entered the lymph capillaries.
quiz.placement: Predict: where does the leaked fluid go? (Images A and B, Kipchoge and the patient with oedema)

quiz.prompt: Kipchoge's leg muscles contract with every stride during a marathon. How does this help to drain extra tissue fluid from his legs and prevent oedema?
choices: The contracting muscles stop the blood capillaries from leaking any plasma at all
The contracting muscles squeeze the lymph vessels, and the valves make the lymph move one way towards the chest
The contracting muscles turn tissue fluid into blood plasma inside the lymph nodes
The contracting muscles make the lymph vessels push lymph back into the blood capillaries of the legs
quiz.rationale: Lymph vessels have valves like veins. Squeezing by contracting muscles pushes lymph along, and the valves stop backflow, so lymph moves towards the chest and excess fluid is drained.
quiz.placement: Activity C: Connecting to the phenomenon (why Kipchoge's legs did not swell during the Berlin Marathon)

quiz.prompt: A learner has tonsillitis and feels swollen, tender lumps under the jaw. What is the main job of the lymph nodes in these lumps?
choices: They filter pathogens from the lymph and make white blood cells that fight infection
They carry lymph directly from the heart to the leg muscles
They store blood to be used during exercise
They pump lymph around the body like a heart
quiz.rationale: Lymph nodes filter pathogens from lymph and contain white blood cells. They swell when fighting an infection such as tonsillitis.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Tracing the lymphatic pathway (lymph nodes in armpits, groin and neck)

quiz.prompt: Mama Zawadi, a fish trader from Kilifi, has lymphatic filariasis. Parasitic worms block her lymph vessels, and her lower legs swell badly. Which explanation for the swelling is correct?
choices: Tissue fluid still leaks from her blood capillaries but cannot drain away through the blocked lymph vessels, so it builds up in the tissues
Her heart is pumping blood backwards into her legs
Her lymph nodes have turned into blood capillaries and make too much plasma
Her blood capillaries have stopped leaking plasma, so the legs fill with air
quiz.rationale: Blood capillaries keep leaking plasma to form tissue fluid. If the lymph vessels are blocked, the fluid cannot be returned to the blood, so it collects in the tissues. This swelling is called oedema.
quiz.placement: Part A: Oedema case study (Mama Zawadi from Kilifi)

quiz.prompt: A grasshopper has an open circulatory system, and it does not have a lymphatic system. Which statement best explains why it does not need one?
choices: Its tracheae carry tissue fluid back to the heart
Its body is too small to lose any fluid
Its heart is stronger than a mammal's heart, so no fluid ever leaks
Its haemolymph bathes the organs directly and is not separated from the tissues by capillary walls, so there is no leaked tissue fluid to drain
quiz.rationale: In an open system the haemolymph is already in direct contact with the tissues. There are no capillaries leaking plasma into a separate tissue fluid compartment, so no lymphatic drainage is needed.
quiz.placement: Part B: Compare with simpler animals (does the grasshopper need a lymphatic system?)

quiz.prompt: Which statement best summarises what the lymphatic system does for the body, including for an athlete like Eliud Kipchoge?
choices: It carries oxygen to the muscles in place of the blood
It replaces the heart when the heart is tired after a race
It drains excess tissue fluid and returns it to the blood, which prevents oedema
It pumps blood faster so that muscles get more oxygen
quiz.rationale: The lymphatic system returns excess tissue fluid (as lymph) to the blood. Without this, fluid would build up in the tissues and cause oedema.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: Lesson 8 evidence card and 'What We Now Know' sticky notes

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the correct route of fluid that leaves the blood capillaries and is returned to the blood by the lymphatic system?
choices: Lymph capillaries, subclavian veins, lymph nodes, thoracic duct
Lymph capillaries, lymph vessels (passing through lymph nodes), thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct, subclavian veins
Subclavian veins, lymph ducts, lymph vessels, lymph capillaries
Blood capillaries, lymph ducts, lymph nodes, tissue spaces
quiz.rationale: Tissue fluid enters blind-ended lymph capillaries and becomes lymph. It flows through lymph vessels and nodes, then into the thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct, which empty into the subclavian veins.
quiz.placement: Cumulative transport model: adding the lymphatic system in green (lymph capillaries to subclavian veins)

lessons.title: The Immune System and Blood Clotting: The Body's Defence and Repair Network

quiz.prompt: A learner predicts that blood clotting happens inside the heart. Where does blood clotting actually take place?
choices: At the damaged blood vessel wall, at the site of the wound
In the lymph nodes, where white cells are stored
In the stomach, where blood is digested
Inside the heart chambers, where blood is pumped
quiz.rationale: Clotting is triggered when a blood vessel wall is damaged, so platelets and clotting factors act at the wound site, not inside the heart.
quiz.placement: Prediction Wall: CLOTTING predictions (Kipchoge's scratched leg)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the correct order of events when a blood vessel is cut?
choices: Thrombin becomes prothrombin, fibrin becomes fibrinogen, platelets aggregate, clot forms
Clot forms, platelets aggregate, fibrinogen becomes fibrin, prothrombin becomes thrombin
Fibrin mesh forms, platelets aggregate, prothrombin becomes thrombin, clot forms
Platelets aggregate at the wound, prothrombin becomes thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, clot forms
quiz.rationale: Platelets gather at the wound and clotting factors are activated. Prothrombin is converted to thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and the fibrin mesh traps red blood cells to form the clot.
quiz.placement: Activity A: The Clotting Cascade Model (yarn and beads Observation Guide)

quiz.prompt: A thorn pierces Amina's finger. Within minutes the area turns red, swells and feels warm, and phagocytes engulf bacteria. Which statement correctly describes this response?
choices: It is a non-specific response because lymphocytes make memory cells
It is a specific response because antibodies are made within minutes
It is a non-specific response because phagocytes act quickly on many kinds of germs and no memory is formed
It is a specific response because it targets only one type of bacteria
quiz.rationale: Phagocytes respond quickly to many types of germs without targeting one pathogen and do not form memory. Antibodies, lymphocytes and memory cells belong to specific immunity.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Immunity Comparison Data Cards (Card 1, non-specific response)

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after a thorn infection, the same bacteria enter Amina's blood and are cleared in 24 hours, much faster than the first time. What best explains this faster response?
choices: Phagocytes become larger after the first infection
Her skin becomes thicker so bacteria cannot enter
Memory cells from B-lymphocytes quickly make antibodies against those bacteria (specific immunity)
Platelets remember the bacteria and destroy them
quiz.rationale: Specific immunity forms memory cells. On the second exposure, B-lymphocytes quickly produce antibodies against the same bacteria, so the infection clears faster.
quiz.placement: Part 2: Immunity Explanation Card (Amina's thorn and bacteria)

quiz.prompt: Achieng, age 12, has malaria. Plasmodium falciparum is destroying her red blood cells and her haemoglobin has dropped from 12 g/dL to 7 g/dL. Her heart beats faster than normal even at rest. Why?
choices: Malaria makes her blood clot too quickly in the heart
Her heart is pumping faster to compensate for fewer red blood cells carrying oxygen
Her heart is fighting the parasite directly with phagocytes
Her heart has grown stronger like an athlete's heart
quiz.rationale: Fewer red blood cells and less haemoglobin means less oxygen is carried per beat. The heart compensates by pumping faster to deliver more oxygen to the tissues.
quiz.placement: Activity C: Malaria Case Study (Achieng's data table)

quiz.prompt: The normal resting heart rate is 75 beats per minute. Achieng, who has malaria, has a resting heart rate of 98 beats per minute. By how many beats per minute is her resting heart rate above normal?
quiz.rationale: 98 − 75 = 23 beats per minute higher than normal.
quiz.placement: Activity C: Malaria Case Study (data table: resting heart rate)

quiz.prompt: Which statement about a grasshopper's haemolymph is correct?
choices: It has no cells that defend the insect against microbes
It clots using a fibrin mesh just like human blood
It has haemocytes that engulf microbes and help seal wounds, but no fibrin clotting, no antibodies and no immune memory
It has lymphocytes that make antibodies and form immune memory
quiz.rationale: Insect haemocytes engulf microbes and help seal wounds in a simpler way. Insects have no fibrin clotting, lymphocytes, antibodies or immune memory.
quiz.placement: Part 3: Connecting to the Phenomenon (grasshopper pivot)

quiz.prompt: In a model of the three roles of blood, TRANSPORT is red, DEFENCE is blue and REPAIR is yellow. Which blood part belongs in the yellow REPAIR group?
choices: Lymphocytes, which make antibodies
Red blood cells, which carry oxygen
Platelets, which start the clotting cascade at a wound
Phagocytes, which engulf bacteria
quiz.rationale: Platelets and the clotting cascade seal wounds, which is the repair role. Red blood cells are transport, and phagocytes and lymphocytes are defence.
quiz.placement: Cumulative Transport System Model: colour-coded legend (TRANSPORT, DEFENCE, REPAIR)

lessons.title: ABO and Rhesus Factor Blood Grouping

quiz.prompt: In a blood typing simulation, vinegar stands in for Anti-A serum and dilute iodine stands in for Anti-B serum. Vinegar fizzes only with the A marker (baking soda) and iodine turns blue-black only with the B marker (starch). A patient sample fizzes when vinegar is added. When iodine is added, it shows only the pale yellow-brown tint of the iodine itself. What is the blood group of this sample?
choices: Group AB
Group A
Group O
Group B
quiz.rationale: The fizz with Anti-A shows the A marker is present. The pale yellow-brown tint is not a blue-black reaction, so there is no B marker. A marker only means group A.
quiz.placement: Part A: Blood Typing Simulation (Anti-A and Anti-B serum on Patient Samples)

quiz.prompt: In the same simulation, a patient sample shows no fizz with 'Anti-A serum' (vinegar) and no blue-black colour with 'Anti-B serum' (iodine). What does this tell you about the sample?
choices: It carries both the A and B markers, so it is group AB
It carries only the B marker, so it is group B
It carries neither the A nor the B marker, so it is group O
The sample is spoiled and the test must be thrown away
quiz.rationale: A reaction shows only when the serum matches a marker in the sample. No reaction with either serum means neither A nor B is present, which is group O. No reaction is a valid result.
quiz.placement: Part A: Blood Typing Simulation (teacher question 'What does NO reaction tell you?')

quiz.prompt: KNBTS data estimate the blood groups of Kenyans as: group O about 46%, group A about 27%, group B about 20% and group AB about 7%. What percentage of Kenyans have a blood group that is NOT group O?
quiz.rationale: Add the other three groups: 27 + 20 + 7 = 54%. This is the same as 100 - 46 = 54%.
quiz.placement: Part B: Kenyan Blood Group Distribution Data (bar chart from the KNBTS data card)

quiz.prompt: An Rh-negative patient needs a blood transfusion. Why should the patient be given Rh-negative blood and not Rh-positive blood?
choices: Rh-negative people always have anti-D antibodies from birth, so no other blood can be used
Rh-negative blood carries more oxygen than Rh-positive blood
Exposure to Rh-positive red cells can make the patient's immune system produce anti-D antibodies that attack Rh-positive red cells
Rh-positive blood has no antigens, so it cannot be used by anyone
quiz.rationale: Rh-positive red cells carry the Rh (D) antigen and Rh-negative cells do not. An Rh-negative person has no anti-D until exposed to Rh-positive blood. After that, the immune system can make anti-D that attacks Rh-positive red cells.
quiz.placement: Part C: Rhesus Factor Mini-Reading (Rh+ and Rh− designations)

quiz.prompt: In real blood, what is agglutination?
choices: The fizzing of blood when it meets an acid
The clumping together of red blood cells when antibodies meet the matching antigens
The breakdown of white blood cells in the lymph
The clotting of blood to seal a wound
quiz.rationale: Agglutination is the clumping of red blood cells when an antibody meets its matching antigen. The simulation only models this match with fizzing or a colour change and does not show clumping.
quiz.placement: Part A: Vocabulary Anchor (Frayer Model for 'agglutination')

quiz.prompt: A patient with blood group A has red cells with A antigens and Anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Which donor blood (ABO groups only) would this patient reject?
choices: Group AB blood
Group O blood
Group A blood
None; a group A patient can safely receive any ABO group
quiz.rationale: Group AB red cells carry the B antigen, which the patient's Anti-B antibodies attack. Group O has no antigens and group A has only A antigens, so both are safe.
quiz.placement: Part B: Transfusion Compatibility Matrix (rule card: 'A recipient has Anti-B antibodies and will reject B or AB donor blood')

quiz.prompt: Why is group O blood called the 'universal donor' for the ABO system?
choices: Its plasma has no antibodies, so it can receive blood from anyone
It is the most common group in Kenya, so it is always available
Its red blood cells carry no A or B antigens, so the recipient's Anti-A or Anti-B antibodies have nothing to attack
It carries both A and B antigens, so it matches every recipient
quiz.rationale: Group O red cells have no A or B antigens, so the recipient's antibodies find no match. Being common is a separate fact. Having no antibodies in the plasma describes group AB, not group O.
quiz.placement: Part B: Transfusion Compatibility Matrix (rule card: 'O donor has no antigens — universal donor')

quiz.prompt: A learner asks: 'Does a grasshopper have blood groups like A, B, AB and O?' Which is the best scientific answer?
choices: No, because a grasshopper's blood is too cold for antigens to form
No, because a grasshopper has haemolymph, not true blood with red blood cells, so there is no ABO system
Yes, because all animals with a heart have the ABO system
Yes, but grasshopper blood groups are not tested because the insects are too small
quiz.rationale: Insects such as grasshoppers have haemolymph and no red blood cells. The ABO antigens are carried on red blood cells, so no ABO system exists in a grasshopper.
quiz.placement: Model revision: comparison note 'Does a grasshopper have blood groups? Why or why not?'

lessons.title: Diversity of Transport Systems: Comparative Overview

quiz.prompt: An Evidence Card says: "Frog ventricle is not fully divided, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix." What does this tell us about the African bullfrog's heart?
choices: Some oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mixes in the single ventricle, so separation is incomplete
Blood passes through the heart only once in each complete circuit
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate
The frog has no blood vessels, so blood mixes freely in the body cavity
quiz.rationale: An undivided ventricle lets oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, so separation is incomplete. This is the amphibian pattern in the comparative table.
quiz.placement: Evidence Cards: read each card aloud and check against notebooks

quiz.prompt: An Evidence Card says: "Grasshopper haemolymph bathes organs directly and does not carry oxygen." Which description of the grasshopper's transport system is correct?
choices: It is a double circulation with a four-chambered heart
It is a single closed circulation in which haemolymph carries oxygen to the muscles
It is a closed system with capillaries linking arteries and veins
It is an open system in which haemolymph flows through the body cavity around the organs
quiz.rationale: Haemolymph is pumped into the body cavity and bathes the organs directly, which is an open system. It does not need to carry oxygen, and an insect's low metabolic demand lets it survive without a closed system.
quiz.placement: Evidence Cards: teacher asks which card explains why a grasshopper can survive without a closed system

quiz.prompt: An Evidence Card says: "Tilapia blood passes through the heart once per complete circuit." Which type of circulation does the Nile tilapia have?
choices: Single closed circulation
Double circulation with mixing in the ventricle
Double circulation with complete separation of blood
Open circulation
quiz.rationale: Blood that passes through the heart once per circuit means single circulation. Fish blood stays inside vessels, so it is closed. Mistaking fish circulation for double is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Comparative Table: completing the fish row (type of circulation)

quiz.prompt: Compare a reptile heart, which has a partial septum in the ventricle, with a frog heart, which has an undivided ventricle. Which statement is correct?
choices: Reptiles have completely separate blood, while frogs have some mixing
Reptiles and frogs have exactly the same amount of mixing
Reptiles have more mixing than frogs because of the partial septum
Reptiles have less mixing than frogs, but the separation is still not complete
quiz.rationale: A partial septum reduces the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood compared with an undivided ventricle. It does not remove the mixing completely, so full separation appears only in mammals.
quiz.placement: Comparative Table: completing the amphibian and reptile rows (separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood)

quiz.prompt: Which description fits the circulatory system of an impala, a mammal?
choices: Open circulation in which blood bathes the organs directly
Double circulation with a single ventricle in which the two kinds of blood mix
Single closed circulation with a two-chambered heart
Double circulation with a four-chambered heart and complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
quiz.rationale: Mammals have a four-chambered heart and double circulation. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are fully separated, which is the third trend drawn out in the whole-class discussion.
quiz.placement: Whole-class discussion: three patterns (open to closed, single to double, incomplete to complete separation)

quiz.prompt: A learner says: "A grasshopper is just a failed mammal, and insects are the ancestors of fish." Which response is the best correction?
choices: The learner is right about insects, but wrong about the grasshopper
The learner is right, because the trends show a ladder from insect to mammal
The learner is wrong, because closed circulation has evolved only once, in mammals
The learner is wrong, because the trends are comparisons, not a ladder. Each system fits its animal's size and energy needs
quiz.rationale: The patterns compare systems and do not show a line of descent. Each system suits its own animal's size and energy demand, and closed circulation evolved more than once, for example in birds and crocodiles as well as mammals.
quiz.placement: Whole-class discussion: the limits of the trend lines ("comparisons, not a ladder")

quiz.prompt: Eliud Kipchoge's heart recovers quickly after a race. Which feature of the mammalian heart best explains how it supports such high energy demand?
choices: Blood passes through the heart only once per circuit, which saves time
Full separation of blood means oxygenated blood reaches the muscles at maximum oxygen concentration without dilution
The heart has a single ventricle, so blood mixes and reaches the muscles faster
Haemolymph bathes his muscles directly, so oxygen reaches them quickly
quiz.rationale: In double circulation with a four-chambered heart, oxygenated blood is not diluted by deoxygenated blood. Muscles therefore receive blood with the maximum oxygen concentration, which supports a high metabolic rate.
quiz.placement: Model update: annotation box "My Explanation of the Phenomenon" (Kipchoge vs a grasshopper's dorsal vessel)

lessons.title: Final Model Presentations & Celebratory Sensemaking: Answering the Driving Question

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the circulatory system of a grasshopper?
choices: Blood flows inside closed vessels and carries oxygen to every cell, as in a mammal
It has an open system: a tube-like pump moves haemolymph, which bathes the organs directly
It has a four-chambered heart that separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
Haemolymph carries oxygen on haemoglobin to the muscles, just like human blood
quiz.rationale: A grasshopper has an open circulatory system with a tube-like heart. Haemolymph is pumped out and surrounds the organs directly, and oxygen reaches cells through tracheal tubes.
quiz.placement: Predict: reading your own Lesson 1 model and writing the sticky-note sentence about what you now understand

quiz.prompt: During a gallery walk, a learner asks: 'Where in the mammalian heart are oxygenated and deoxygenated blood kept apart?' Which answer is correct?
choices: They are kept apart by haemolymph surrounding the heart
They mix in the ventricles and are separated later in the lungs
A wall (septum) divides the left side of the heart from the right side, so the two kinds of blood do not mix
They are separated only by the valves in the veins
quiz.rationale: The mammalian heart has separate left and right sides divided by a septum. This lets double circulation keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.
quiz.placement: Gallery walk: 'Two Stars and a Wondering' sticky-note protocol

quiz.prompt: Eliud Kipchoge sustains world-record speeds and recovers quickly after a race. Which explanation best uses the idea of double circulation?
choices: Oxygenated blood is kept separate from deoxygenated blood and pumped under pressure to his muscles, so oxygen delivery is efficient
His heart is so large that it does not need to beat faster during a race
His blood does not need oxygen when he runs fast
His blood bathes his muscles directly, as haemolymph does in a grasshopper
quiz.rationale: Double circulation separates oxygenated from deoxygenated blood, so the blood sent to the muscles carries a lot of oxygen. This supports sustained aerobic activity and fast recovery.
quiz.placement: Group presentations: directly answering the driving question 'Kipchoge can sustain world-record speeds and recover fast BECAUSE...'

quiz.prompt: A learner's pulse rate was 72 beats per minute at rest and 138 beats per minute after star jumps. By how many beats per minute did the pulse rate increase?
quiz.rationale: Increase = pulse after exercise minus resting pulse = 138 - 72 = 66 beats per minute. The heart beats faster to meet the higher oxygen demand of the muscles.
quiz.placement: Final Written Explanation (CER): citing evidence from the pulse-rate experiment

quiz.prompt: In the surface-area-to-volume (SA:V) investigation with cubes, a cube with sides of 2 cm has an SA:V ratio of 3. A larger cube has sides of 4 cm (surface area 96 cm², volume 64 cm³). What is the SA:V ratio of the 4 cm cube, and what does this suggest about large animals?
choices: 24; larger bodies lose oxygen faster, so they do not need a transport system
1.5; larger bodies have less surface area for their volume, so they need a transport system
3; the ratio stays the same, so size does not affect transport needs
6; larger bodies have more surface area for their volume, so diffusion alone is enough
quiz.rationale: SA:V = 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5, which is lower than 3. As bodies get larger, surface area compared with volume falls, so diffusion alone cannot supply every cell and a transport system is needed.
quiz.placement: Final Explanation: evidence from the SA:V cube calculations

quiz.prompt: During the DQB audit, the class decides that the question 'Why does the heart beat faster during exercise?' is ANSWERED. Which piece of evidence best supports this?
choices: A pulse rose from 72 to 138 beats per minute after star jumps, showing the heart pumps faster when muscles need more oxygen
The heart is about the size of a fist
A grasshopper has a tube-like heart
Eliud Kipchoge is a famous marathon runner
quiz.rationale: Measured pulse-rate data before and after exercise is direct evidence linking a faster heart rate to greater oxygen demand. The other statements are true or unrelated, but they do not answer the question.
quiz.placement: DQB audit: thumbs vote and one-sentence evidence citation for ANSWERED questions

quiz.prompt: Imagine Eliud Kipchoge had the circulatory system of a grasshopper. What would most likely happen during a marathon?
choices: He would run faster, because haemolymph reaches the muscles directly
Nothing would change, because all animals have the same transport needs
His muscles would be better supplied, because an open system holds more blood
He could not sustain the speed, because an open system cannot deliver oxygen to his muscles fast enough for such high demand
quiz.rationale: In an open system the fluid just bathes the tissues and is not pumped quickly through closed vessels. This cannot meet the high oxygen demand of sustained marathon running.
quiz.placement: Organism voice role-play and the final reading of the driving question

quiz.prompt: In the tilapia column of the class consensus model, how many times does blood pass through the heart in one complete circuit of the body?
choices: Twice, because fish have double circulation
Not at all, because fish blood is not pumped by a heart
Once, because fish have single circulation
Four times, because fish have four heart chambers
quiz.rationale: A tilapia has a closed system with single circulation, so blood passes through the heart once in each complete circuit. Mammals such as Kipchoge have double circulation, with blood passing through the heart twice.
quiz.placement: Class Consensus Model: TILAPIA (Lake Victoria) column, single/double circulation arrows
